target_customer: Plastic and reconstructive surgeons (breast and facial reconstruction) who rebuild tissue from a patient's own fat
problem: Fat grafts partly reabsorb and synthetic implants and fillers carry drawbacks, so surgeons lack a reliable way to rebuild volume with the patient's own tissue.
business_model: Regulated medical device and biomaterial (Fractomer Biomatrix) developed with grant funding, intended for sale to surgeons and hospitals
product_category: Synthetic biology biomaterial for soft tissue reconstruction

founders.name: Stefan Roberts
education: Duke University, PhD in Biomedical Engineering (2018)
Washington University in St. Louis, began undergraduate studies in biomedical engineering (degree not stated in the Duke article)
founders.background_notes: Developed the core technology in his Duke dissertation (company team page, Duke Capital Partners article). Summer research at St. Jude and Barnes-Jewish Hospital per the Duke article.

founders.name: Scott Hollenbeck
prior_employers: Duke University (Director of Breast Reconstruction at the time)
founders.background_notes: Called co-founder in the Duke Capital Partners article; the company site lists him as lead medical advisor and chair of UVA plastic surgery. Not on the YC page.

founders.name: Ashutosh Chilkoti
founders.background_notes: The YC page lists him as a founder; the Duke Capital Partners article describes him as Roberts's PhD advisor and does not call him a co-founder.

technical_complexity.rationale: Recombinant protein polymer that gels at body temperature and must pass device regulation; the company site describes it as built on protein sequences found in the human body, and the 2024 BIO listing calls the product pre-clinical.

defensibility.rationale: Technology licensed from Duke research and protected by the regulatory path for a new biomaterial; a rival would need years of development and clinical data.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent was found building the same recombinant matrix. The Duke article contrasts the product with silicone implants and large tissue transfer, not with a named company.

market_need_then: Surgeons use liposuctioned fat and implants for reconstruction after cancer treatment; the company pitches half the fat and twice the structure. NIH and NSF grants totalling more than $3 million indicate scientific reviewers saw need.

identity.logo: Wordmark inSoma Bio; not described in sources
identity.voice_and_tone: Scientific and patient focused; slogan Rebuilding You With You

branding.brand_signature: Slogan Rebuilding You With You and the Fractomer product name

brand_strength.rationale: A memorable slogan and product name, but a B2B medical audience and no press about the brand itself.

outcome_analysis: inSoma Bio is a Duke spinout that has funded itself mostly through Duke Capital Partners, SEC-reported small private raises in 2020, and NIH and NSF grants of more than $3 million. By 2025 it joined the MedTech Innovator program and reports no exit. Progress depends on clinical and regulatory milestones, so the company is still a long dated science bet rather than a commercial success or failure.
notes: The October 2020 Research Triangle article lists $200,000 (latest, from an SEC filing), $110,000 in September and $200,000 in July 2020 with $690,000 still sought; only the latest is recorded as a round. The grant amounts (over $2M NCI, $1M NSF) are stated by the Duke article, whose date is not given and are recorded without dates. Aggregator seed figures of $1.9M and $2.7M in 2025 and 2026 and a $7.8M total are unverified and conflict. A $250k NC Biotech Center loan and a NSF grant of about $253K appear in search snippets only. Competitor list is empty because no source dated near the 2020 batch was found; Renuva (MTF Biologics) and similar fat matrices appeared only in undated pages. Exit none; no layoffs or shutdown found. Duke article says a third co-founder exists but is unnamed.
